title: Afghanistan: Land of High Mountains, Kite Fights, and Snow Leopards
summary:
Imagine a country where kids fly kites that have wire or glass on the strings—so they can cut their rivals' kite strings in a battle. That's Afghanistan, a country in Central Asia. It sits between Iran to the west and Pakistan to the east.

Most of Afghanistan is covered in tall, jagged mountains and dry deserts. The peaks are snow-covered for most of the year. Many people live in fertile valleys between the mountains, where they grow crops and tend animals. Only 20 percent of the land is used as fields. Summers are hot and dry, but winters are very cold, especially north of the Hindu Kush mountains.

Afghanistan has many different groups of people. About 15 million people, nearly half the population, are Pashtuns. They live in the south around Kandahar. Other groups include Tajiks, Uzbeks, and Hazaras. The country was once a busy part of the Silk Road, a route merchants traveled between China, India, and Europe for over 2,000 years.

Tea is the favorite drink. A popular meal is palau, made from rice, sheep and goat meat, and fruit. Sadly, decades of war have left unexploded mines in the countryside. Many schools have been destroyed, but children, including girls, still go to school wherever they can.

Wildlife has suffered too. Tigers used to roam the hills, but they are now extinct. Endangered snow leopards still live in the cold Hindu Kush, relying on their thick fur to stay warm.
why_it_matters: Learning about a country far away helps you understand why its land, its long history, and even its animals matter to the people who live there.

background_read: Afghanistan (a country in Central Asia, filled with mountains and deserts) has been a crossroads where travelers and traders have passed for thousands of years.
The Silk Road (old trade routes linking China, India, and Europe) carried silk, spices, and new ideas across Asia, and part of it ran through Afghanistan.
Snow leopards (big grey cats with thick fur) live high in the mountains of Central Asia and are endangered, which means only a few are left in the wild.
Article_Structure: WHO: The people of Afghanistan, including Pashtuns, Tajiks, Uzbeks, and Hazaras, plus the children who still go to school.
WHAT: A look at the country's mountains, deserts, valleys, foods, kite fights, history, and wildlife.
WHERE: Afghanistan, in Central Asia, between Iran and Pakistan, with the Hindu Kush mountains in the north.
WHY: The story shows how the land and a long, hard history shape everyday life — from farming in the valleys to endangered snow leopards in the cold mountains.

perspectives.description: Kite fights with glass-coated strings, cups of tea, and big plates of palau show how rich and old Afghan traditions are.
Decades of war left unexploded mines in the countryside and destroyed many schools, which makes daily life dangerous and hard.
Tigers have already disappeared from Afghanistan, but snow leopards still survive in the Hindu Kush thanks to their thick fur.
